$why_source: The canonical copy lives at the path above. Every other language VENDORS this file byte for byte and is found by this field rather than by a list somebody maintains, the same way C2 finds a vendored schema by its $id.
comment: Cross-language pinned vectors for the agent-passport SPEC 5 delegation chain: the MAPPING from an RFC 8693 token to `on_behalf_of`, and the three rules a chain must satisfy. Every DOOR (Go: this repo's delegation package; Rust: tokenfuse's crates/delegation) and every RECORD (Go: this repo's chain package) MUST answer each case the same way. `sub` and `act` are the token's claims, `act` written outermost-first as RFC 8693 nests it. `chain` is the assembled `on_behalf_of`, root first, and is present only when the verdict is `accept`. `verdict` is `accept` or the rule that refuses. A door refuses by returning its own error; the vector names the RULE, not the error type, because the three languages spell their errors differently and the rule is the thing that must agree. A vector may name `act_generated` instead of `act`: `{template, count}` expands to `count` actors, the template's `%d` replaced by 1..count. It keeps the depth cases readable rather than listing thirty-three URIs, and every language expands it the same way.

rules.accept: The chain is well formed and every rule holds.
rules.cycle: SPEC 5.1: the chain MUST be acyclic. One principal named twice.
rules.too_deep: SPEC 5.1: maximum chain depth is 32 ENTRIES, and the subject is one of them.

vectors.name: the shape every real token has
vectors.why: One human, one agent. If a change makes this refuse, it refuses every token this estate mints.

vectors.name: the mapping is a reversal, not a copy
vectors.why: RFC 8693 nests current-first and the estate records root-first. A door that skipped the reversal would produce a chain that verifies and asserts the opposite of what happened.

vectors.name: no subject, so the actors are the whole chain
vectors.why: A machine-to-machine chain has no human at the root. The whole entry budget belongs to the actors, and a door that reserved a slot for an absent subject would refuse a chain the SPEC allows.

vectors.name: the subject is also an actor
vectors.why: The trap `BuildAct` invites: its doc example passes a whole root-first chain, root included, so the root lands inside `act` while also being the token's `sub`.

vectors.name: one actor named twice
vectors.why: The rule is about the assembled chain, not only about the subject.

vectors.name: a principal that is not a principal
vectors.why: The v0.2 envelope pins `pattern: ^(agent|user)://` on every item of `on_behalf_of`, so anything else is a record nobody can write.

vectors.name: a scheme one character short
vectors.why: `agent:/` is not `agent://`. A prefix check written by hand gets this wrong in one direction or the other.

vectors.name: an empty principal
vectors.why: Refused by every implementation already, and here so that a rewrite cannot lose it.

vectors.name: the subject plus thirty-one actors is exactly the cap
vectors.why: SPEC 5.1 counts ENTRIES and the subject is one. This is the largest chain the estate accepts, and a door that bounded actors at 32 would accept one more.

vectors.name: the subject plus thirty-two actors is one too many
vectors.why: The off-by-one measured on 2026-08-27: this verified at both doors and every record it produced was quarantined as 33 entries.

vectors.name: with no subject the actors get the whole budget
vectors.why: Thirty-two actors and no human is thirty-two entries, which is the cap and not over it. The mirror of the case above, and the one a fix that overshot would refuse.
